name: Sulaiman (Solomon)
source: Stories of the Prophets — compiled from the Qur'an and authentic hadith
paras: Sulaiman was the son of Dawud, inheriting from his father both the kingdom and the prophethood — a combination given to no one else in such fullness: "And Sulaiman inherited Dawud." (An-Naml 27:16). He said: "O people, we have been taught the language of birds, and we have been given from all things. Indeed, this is evident bounty."

When the two judgments of Dawud were retried by Sulaiman, Allah affirmed the finer verdict: "And We made Sulaiman understand it; and to each We gave judgment and knowledge." (Al-Anbiya 21:79) — yet the same verse seals both prophets from pride: they were doers of good.

His kingdom was not like the kingdoms of men: the wind was made subject to him — "flowing by his command toward the land which We had blessed" (Al-Anbiya 21:81) — and the devils were bound to build and dive for him.

The ants taught the first lesson of his reign. Marching with his hosts, he smiled at the speech of an ant warning her colony: "O ants, enter your dwellings that you be not crushed by Sulaiman and his soldiers while they perceive not." He prayed at once: "My Lord, enable me to be grateful for Your favour which You have bestowed upon me and upon my parents..." (An-Naml 27:18-19).

The hoopoe brought him news of Saba' in Yemen — a sun-worshipping queen on a magnificent throne. Sulaiman sent the letter: "Indeed, it is from Sulaiman, and indeed it reads: 'In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful: Be not haughty with me but come to me in submission.'" (An-Naml 27:30-31).

Bilqis, the Queen of Sheba, tested him with gifts; he answered: "Do you provide me with wealth? Rather, what Allah has given me is better than what He has given you." (An-Naml 27:36). Then, shown the truth — his own throne brought in the blink of an eye, a palace of glass under which water flowed — she declared: "My Lord, indeed I have wronged myself, and I submit with Sulaiman to Allah, Lord of the worlds." (An-Naml 27:44).

The Qur'an insists he never disbelieved — the devils did, teaching people magic (Al-Baqarah 2:102). His death itself was a sign of the unseen: he passed leaning on his staff, and the jinn continued their labour until a termite gnawed it and he fell — "when he fell, it became clear to the jinn that if they had known the unseen, they would not have remained in humiliating punishment." (Saba' 34:14).

Sulaiman's story is the Qur'an's portrait of power without corruption: a kingdom of wind and jinn and birds held by a servant who prayed, "My Lord, forgive me and grant me a kingdom such as will not belong to any after me. Indeed, You are the Bestower." (Sad 38:35).
